cards.heading: What actually makes something an agent
cards.hook: An agent perceives its environment, reasons about a goal, acts through tools, and adapts from feedback — a chatbot that only responds to one prompt at a time is missing most of that loop.

cards.heading: Agent vs chatbot in one line
cards.hook: A chatbot responds to what you ask; an agent takes initiative toward a goal across multiple steps, with tools and persistent memory a chatbot doesn't have.

cards.heading: Simple reflex agents react, nothing more
cards.hook: A spam filter is a simple reflex agent: it follows condition-action rules on the current input with zero memory of anything that came before.

cards.heading: Model-based agents remember the world
cards.hook: A model-based agent keeps an internal picture of state, like a personal assistant tracking your preferences, so its decisions use history, not just the current input.

cards.heading: Goal-based vs utility-based agents
cards.hook: A goal-based agent just works toward an objective; a utility-based agent scores and balances several competing objectives at once, like an investment advisor weighing risk against return.

cards.heading: The five-step loop under almost every agent
cards.hook: Observe, think, act, evaluate, repeat — strip away the framework-specific jargon and nearly every agent architecture is a variation on this same cycle.

cards.heading: What actually enables modern agents
cards.hook: Function calling bridges language and real actions, vector databases give agents semantic memory, and orchestration frameworks like LangChain just provide scaffolding around both.

cards.heading: The five hard problems every agent hits
cards.hook: Reliability, cost, latency, safety, and evaluation — these don't go away with a better prompt, they're structural to how agents work.

cards.heading: Multi-step reasoning is expensive by construction
cards.hook: Every additional reasoning step in an agent loop is another LLM call, so the same flexibility that makes agents powerful is also what makes them slow and costly.

cards.heading: What you actually need to build your first agent
cards.hook: LLM API access, a tool set, a clear success criteria, and an evaluation method — skipping the evaluation method is the most common first mistake.

cards.heading: Every agent is the same few components wired together
cards.hook: LLM backend, tool executor, memory system, and a controller that orchestrates them — nearly every agent framework is just a different wiring of these four pieces.

cards.heading: Temperature is a tool-selection dial, not just a creativity dial
cards.hook: Low temperature, around 0 to 0.3, is what you want for tool selection and reasoning; high temperature is for brainstorming, not for deciding which function to call.

cards.heading: A tool is a name, a description, and a function
cards.hook: The description is what the LLM actually reads to decide when to call a tool — a vague description is the single most common reason an agent picks the wrong tool.

cards.heading: A tool registry is just a lookup the prompt is built from
cards.hook: get_tool_descriptions() formats every registered tool into text the LLM reads before deciding what to call — the registry IS the agent's available-actions list.

cards.heading: Short-term memory has to actively forget
cards.hook: Working memory holds the current conversation up to a token budget, and once that budget is hit it has to actively trim the oldest messages.

cards.heading: Long-term memory means embeddings plus a vector store
cards.hook: Storing something in long-term memory means converting it to an embedding first, so retrieval later becomes a nearest-neighbor search over meaning, not keyword matching.

cards.heading: Episodic memory records what happened, not just facts
cards.hook: Episodic memory stores the specific state, action, and result of past attempts, which lets an agent search for similar past situations instead of past facts.

cards.heading: A planner just turns one goal into many subtasks
cards.hook: Task decomposition is literally asking the LLM to break a goal into a numbered list of steps — the hard part is parsing and validating that list reliably, not generating it.

cards.heading: Selecting an action is really just scoring every option
cards.hook: A decision maker evaluates every available action against the current goal and picks the highest-scoring one — expensive if evaluation itself needs an LLM call per option.

cards.heading: The controller is the only piece that runs the loop
cards.hook: Every other component, memory, tools, planner, is passive until the controller's run loop calls observe, decide, execute, and update in sequence.

cards.heading: Keep agent components loosely coupled
cards.hook: Modularity, per-component error handling, and logging every component interaction are what make an agent debuggable — a monolithic agent class is a black box the moment something breaks.

cards.heading: ReAct interleaves thinking and acting
cards.hook: Thought, Action, Observation, repeat — ReAct's whole trick is forcing the model to reason explicitly before every single tool call, which is what makes its output interpretable.

cards.heading: ReAct's biggest weakness is its own verbosity
cards.hook: Because every step needs its own LLM call and its own written-out thought, ReAct can burn through tokens fast and occasionally loop without converging on an answer.

cards.heading: Plan first, execute second — a different tradeoff than ReAct
cards.hook: Plan-and-Execute commits to a full plan upfront, which makes progress trackable and steps parallelizable, but makes the agent less adaptive when an early result changes everything.

cards.heading: Reflexion agents learn by writing down what went wrong
cards.hook: After a failed attempt, a Reflexion agent generates a written reflection on why it failed and feeds that into its next attempt — memory of failure, not just a retry.

cards.heading: Reflexion trades cost for robustness
cards.hook: Multiple attempts mean multiple LLM calls before success, so Reflexion is the right call for debugging and problem-solving tasks, not for anything latency-sensitive.

cards.heading: Hierarchical vs peer-to-peer multi-agent systems
cards.hook: A hierarchical system has one manager delegating to specialized workers; a peer-to-peer system has agents negotiating as equals — hierarchical is far easier to debug.

cards.heading: Specialization is the whole point of multi-agent systems
cards.hook: A product manager agent, an architect agent, and a QA agent each doing one thing well is the same reason human teams specialize, at the cost of coordination overhead.

cards.heading: TAG uses tools to fact-check generation, not to reason
cards.hook: Instead of a full reasoning loop, Tool-Augmented Generation drops tool-call placeholders directly into generated text and fills them in afterward — cheap, and good enough when tools only verify facts.

cards.heading: SOAR splits memory into four separate kinds
cards.hook: Working, procedural, episodic, and semantic memory as four distinct stores is SOAR's core idea — borrowed straight from cognitive science, not from LLM engineering.

cards.heading: Match the architecture to the task, not the hype
cards.hook: ReAct for general QA, Plan-and-Execute for structured workflows, Reflexion for debugging-style tasks, Multi-Agent only when the complexity truly justifies the cost.

cards.heading: Multi-agent is the most expensive architecture by far
cards.hook: More agents means more LLM calls means more cost and coordination overhead — reach for multi-agent only when a single agent's quality genuinely isn't enough.

cards.heading: Production agents rarely use just one architecture
cards.hook: A real agent often plans like Plan-and-Execute, executes each step with ReAct, and falls back to Reflexion when a step fails — named architectures are building blocks, not a menu.

cards.heading: A reasoning trace is also a debugging tool
cards.hook: Because ReAct writes out every thought before acting, you can read exactly where its reasoning went wrong — architectures that skip this step save tokens but lose that visibility.

cards.heading: Tool use is a four-step cycle, not a single API call
cards.hook: Recognize a tool is needed, generate the call, execute it, then incorporate the result back into reasoning — skipping the last step is why some agents call a tool and ignore what it returned.

cards.heading: A tool's description is the only thing the model actually reads
cards.hook: The model never sees your function's implementation — only the name, description, and parameter schema, so a vague description is invisible to you but crippling to the model.

cards.heading: OpenAI and Claude format tool calls differently
cards.hook: OpenAI returns tool_calls as a separate array alongside content; Claude embeds tool_use blocks directly inside the content array — same idea, incompatible wire formats.
cards.code:
# OpenAI: response.choices[0].message.tool_calls
# Claude: response.content filtered for type == 'tool_use'

cards.heading: Models without native function calling still need a format
cards.hook: TOOL: tool_name / ARGS: {...} as a plain-text convention is how you fake function calling on a model that doesn't support it natively.

cards.heading: Validate before you execute, every time
cards.hook: Checking a tool exists, validating its required parameters, and enforcing a timeout are the three checks that turn a reckless tool call into a safe one.

cards.heading: A timeout on a tool call is not optional
cards.hook: A tool call with no timeout can hang the entire agent loop indefinitely — wrapping every execution in a hard timeout is the cheapest insurance against a single bad tool.

cards.heading: Sandboxing means isolating what a tool can touch
cards.hook: Running a tool inside a container or isolated process with resource limits is what keeps one tool's failure, or abuse, from reaching the rest of the system.

cards.heading: A composite tool is a workflow dressed up as one tool
cards.hook: A composite tool executes a whole sequence of sub-tools and threads their outputs through shared context — from the LLM's point of view it's still just one tool call.

cards.heading: Streaming tools yield results incrementally
cards.hook: A tool that yields chunks as it works, instead of blocking until fully done, lets an agent start reasoning about partial results before the whole operation finishes.

cards.heading: A bad tool description reads like a man page nobody wrote
cards.hook: 'query db' tells the model nothing; naming exactly what a tool returns, what it's for, and what it's not for is what drives correct tool selection.

cards.heading: A tool's error message should suggest the fix
cards.hook: Returning a raw exception to the model wastes a turn; returning an error plus a concrete suggestion lets the model self-correct on the next call.

cards.heading: Rate limit tools the same way you'd rate limit an API
cards.hook: A tool with no per-minute cap lets a confused agent hammer it in a loop — rate limiting a tool is the same discipline as rate limiting any external API, for the same reason.

cards.heading: Four memory types cover almost everything an agent needs
cards.hook: Short-term for the current task, long-term for durable facts, episodic for past experiences, procedural for how to do things — most memory bugs come from using the wrong one.

cards.heading: Working memory has to actively discard the oldest messages
cards.hook: Once a conversation's token count passes its budget, trimming from the oldest message forward is the only way to stay inside a fixed context window.

cards.heading: Summarize before you discard, not instead of discarding
cards.hook: A sliding window keeps recent messages in full but replaces older ones with an LLM-generated summary — you lose detail, not the thread of what happened.

cards.heading: Long-term memory retrieval is a similarity search, not a lookup
cards.hook: Storing content as an embedding means retrieving it later is embed the query, find the nearest vectors — which is why phrasing a query differently from how it was stored still works.

cards.heading: A knowledge graph stores relationships, a vector store stores meaning
cards.hook: Subject, predicate, object triples in a graph let you ask what's connected to X within two hops — a question a pure vector store genuinely can't answer.

cards.heading: Episodic memory is what makes an agent learn from specific mistakes
cards.hook: Recording context, action, result, and success per attempt lets an agent later search for situations similar to right now and recall what actually worked.

cards.heading: Reinforced episodic memory turns outcomes into Q-values
cards.hook: Attaching a reward to each recorded episode and updating a running Q-value per state-action pair is a lightweight way to bias future action choice toward past successes.

cards.heading: Procedural memory stores how, not what
cards.hook: A stored procedure with its own success rate and usage count lets an agent reuse a sequence of steps that's worked before instead of re-deriving the same plan from scratch.

cards.heading: An integrated memory system routes, it doesn't replace
cards.hook: remember() classifying content into short-term, long-term, episodic, or procedural, and recall() querying several at once, is what a production memory system actually looks like.

cards.heading: Consolidation moves the important stuff from short-term to long-term
cards.hook: Just like sleep consolidation in humans, an agent can periodically scan working memory, decide what's worth keeping, and move only that into long-term storage.

cards.heading: Prune old memories or they silently degrade retrieval quality
cards.hook: A memory store that only ever grows eventually buries useful recent context under years of low-value entries — pruning by age and access count keeps retrieval sharp.

cards.heading: Sensitive memories need encryption, not just access control
cards.hook: Marking a stored memory as high-sensitivity and encrypting its content before it hits the vector store is the difference between a privacy control and a comment in the code.

cards.heading: Specific beats clever every time
cards.hook: 'Do something with this data' produces nothing useful; naming the exact file, the exact calculations, and the exact tools to use is what gets a correct result.

cards.heading: A system prompt needs company context, not just a role
cards.hook: Telling an agent it's a support agent isn't enough — it needs the product, the customer segment, the common issues, and exactly when to escalate to a human.

cards.heading: Structure the prompt to force reasoning before action
cards.hook: Explicitly asking what information is needed, which tool fits, and what's the sequence before the task is attempted produces visibly better tool selection than just stating the task.

cards.heading: The ReAct prompt format is just a reusable template
cards.hook: Thought, Action, Action Input, Observation, repeated, with a final-answer slot at the end, IS the entire ReAct architecture expressed as a prompt string.

cards.heading: Plan-and-Execute needs two separate prompts, not one
cards.hook: A planning prompt produces the step list; a separate execution prompt runs one step at a time with access to prior results — conflating the two tends to produce plans that never get followed.

cards.heading: Few-shot examples teach format, not just content
cards.hook: Three worked examples of error-to-fix before the real question isn't about teaching facts — it's about locking the model into the exact output shape you want back.

cards.heading: Chain-of-thought works by naming the steps, not just saying think
cards.hook: A six-step scaffold — understand, list knowns, list unknowns, choose approach, execute, verify — gets more reliable reasoning than simply asking a model to think step by step.

cards.heading: Self-consistency catches an answer that only looked right
cards.hook: Generating three independent reasoning paths and comparing their answers surfaces a wrong answer that would've looked perfectly confident if you'd only generated one.

cards.heading: Make the model argue for each tool before picking one
cards.hook: Walking through would this tool help, and why, for every candidate before committing to one measurably reduces wrong-tool selections compared to just asking which tool to use.

cards.heading: An error-recovery prompt should ask if retrying even makes sense
cards.hook: Not every failure is retryable — a good recovery prompt makes the model explicitly decide whether to retry with different parameters, try a different approach, or escalate.

cards.heading: Meta-prompting is using an agent to fix another agent's prompt
cards.hook: Feeding a prompt's failure rate and common failure modes into a second LLM call that suggests improvements turns prompt tuning into something you can automate, not just guess at.

cards.heading: Dumping fifty tools into one prompt backfires
cards.hook: A flat list of fifty tool descriptions overwhelms tool selection — grouping into core tools, data tools, and rarely-needed admin tools gets the model to the right one faster.

cards.heading: Multi-agent systems exist for five concrete reasons
cards.hook: Specialization, scalability, robustness to single-agent failure, modularity, and parallelization — reach for multi-agent only when one of these five actually applies.

cards.heading: Hierarchical multi-agent is a manager delegating to workers
cards.hook: A manager agent decomposes the task, assigns subtasks to specialized workers, validates each result, and can reassign on failure — the shape of a human engineering team.

cards.heading: Peer-to-peer agents negotiate instead of being assigned
cards.hook: Agents without a manager propose approaches, share them with peers, and synthesize a combined plan — more flexible than hierarchical, and much harder to keep from talking past each other.

cards.heading: A pipeline is the simplest multi-agent pattern there is
cards.hook: Outliner, then writer, then editor, then fact-checker, then formatter — each agent only handles the previous one's output, which makes a pipeline trivial to debug stage by stage.

cards.heading: Debate systems make agents argue until they converge
cards.hook: Agents state a position, see each other's positions, and get another round to revise — useful when a decision needs stress-testing from multiple angles before it's committed to.

cards.heading: Auction-based systems let agents bid for work
cards.hook: Each agent scores its own fit for a task and the highest bid wins — a lightweight way to route tasks to whichever agent is best suited, without a hardcoded assignment.

cards.heading: A message bus decouples agents from knowing about each other directly
cards.hook: Agents send messages to a central bus by recipient name, not to each other's objects directly, which is what lets you add or remove an agent without rewiring every other one.

cards.heading: Shared memory between agents needs locking, same as any shared resource
cards.hook: Letting two agents write to the same memory key without a lock is a race condition with extra steps — acquire, write, release, exactly like guarding any shared mutable state.

cards.heading: Centralized coordination is easier to reason about than decentralized
cards.hook: A single coordinator building a dependency graph and assigning ready tasks is simpler to debug than agents independently negotiating and risking conflicting commitments.

cards.heading: A healthy multi-agent system assumes an agent will fail
cards.hook: Tracking per-agent health and falling back to the next healthy agent on timeout or exception is what keeps one bad agent from taking down the whole system.

cards.heading: Define each agent's role, expertise, and constraints explicitly
cards.hook: Only use reliable sources and must provide citations as explicit constraints on a researcher agent prevent exactly the kind of unsourced claim a vague role definition invites.

cards.heading: Conflicting agent outputs need an explicit resolution strategy
cards.hook: Majority vote for boolean outputs, confidence-weighted averaging when scores exist, escalation to a meta-agent otherwise — pick the strategy before the conflict happens, not during it.

cards.heading: Task success rate is the metric that actually matters first
cards.hook: Before measuring cost, speed, or elegance, the only question that matters is whether the agent actually accomplished the goal — everything else is a secondary optimization.

cards.heading: Efficiency metrics catch an agent that succeeds the expensive way
cards.hook: Steps taken versus optimal steps, tokens per step, and redundant tool calls surface an agent that completes tasks but burns far more cost than it needs to.

cards.heading: Using an LLM as judge needs explicit scoring criteria
cards.hook: Asking a model to score output on correctness, completeness, and clarity, one criterion at a time with reasoning, produces far more consistent scores than a single vague rate this 1-10.

cards.heading: A reasoning trace can be scored for more than the final answer
cards.hook: Logical consistency, whether each step moves closer to the goal, and how much backtracking happened are all measurable independent of whether the final answer was right.

cards.heading: Unit test agent components in isolation, not just the whole agent
cards.hook: Testing a single tool's execution and a single memory store's retrieve function separately catches bugs that a full end-to-end agent test would bury under unrelated noise.

cards.heading: Integration tests should assert on the trace, not just the output
cards.hook: Checking that a multi-step task made at least three tool calls, not just that the final string looks right, actually verifies multi-step reasoning happened instead of a lucky guess.

cards.heading: A benchmark suite needs categories, not just more test cases
cards.hook: Reasoning, tool use, knowledge, planning, and robustness as separate benchmark categories tell you where an agent is weak — one mixed pile just gives you one number.

cards.heading: An automated evaluation pipeline runs every metric on every test case
cards.hook: Success, efficiency, quality, and reasoning evaluators running against the same test suite in one pass turns evaluation into something you re-run on every change, not a one-off script.

cards.heading: Human evaluation should ask concrete questions, not is this good
cards.hook: Is it correct, how helpful on a 1-5 scale, is it well formatted — specific, structured questions produce evaluations you can actually aggregate across many raters.

cards.heading: Monitor success rate as a rolling average, not a lifetime total
cards.hook: A rolling average over the last 100 executions catches a regression within minutes; a lifetime total success rate can hide a brand new problem for days.

cards.heading: Direct injection just asks the model to ignore its instructions
cards.hook: Ignore previous instructions, typed straight into user input, is the simplest attack there is — and it still works on agents that don't explicitly defend against it.

cards.heading: Indirect injection hides instructions inside data the agent reads
cards.hook: A hidden instruction buried inside a document the agent is summarizing is more dangerous than a direct attack, because the agent never expected the document to be adversarial.

cards.heading: Wrap user input in explicit boundaries the model is told to distrust
cards.hook: BEGIN USER INPUT and END USER INPUT markers, plus an instruction to treat anything inside as data not commands, is the standard defense against both direct and indirect injection.

cards.heading: Every tool needs its own permission level, not a blanket allow
cards.hook: Registering a tool with a required permission and a risk level means a high-risk tool like delete_database can demand approval that a read-only search tool never needs.

cards.heading: Validate a generated SQL query before you ever run it
cards.hook: Rejecting anything that isn't a SELECT, blocking dangerous keywords like DROP and DELETE, and checking for injection patterns is what keeps a query tool from becoming a drop-the-database tool.

cards.heading: Scan agent output for PII before it ever reaches the user
cards.hook: Emails, phone numbers, credit card numbers, and API keys all match simple patterns — scanning and redacting them from output is cheap insurance against accidental leakage.

cards.heading: An agent needs per-hour limits, not just per-call limits
cards.hook: Tracking tokens, API calls, and cost per agent with an hourly reset is what stops a stuck loop from quietly running up an unbounded bill overnight.

cards.heading: Human-in-the-loop for anything irreversible
cards.hook: A payment, a database delete, or a sent email are exactly the kinds of action worth pausing for explicit human approval — anything reversible doesn't need the friction.

cards.heading: Constrain the action space instead of trusting good behavior
cards.hook: Telling an agent you can ONLY use these tools, and validating its output against that exact allowlist, is a stronger guarantee than hoping the model just behaves.

cards.heading: A read-only agent is a whole category of risk eliminated
cards.hook: Filtering an agent's tool set down to only read-only tools at construction time means there's no code path left where it could modify or delete anything, by design.

cards.heading: Audit logs need to be append-only, not just present
cards.hook: A log an agent, or an attacker, could edit after the fact isn't really an audit trail — appending every tool execution to an immutable log is what makes incident review trustworthy.

cards.heading: Anomaly detection compares behavior against a baseline, not a rule
cards.hook: Flagging an unusual tool-call sequence or an execution time three times the baseline catches novel misuse that a fixed rule list was never written to anticipate.

cards.heading: Containment comes before investigation, always
cards.hook: Suspend the agent, revoke its credentials, and block its network access first — figuring out what happened can wait until it can no longer do more damage.

cards.heading: Start with the simplest possible agent, then add one capability at a time
cards.hook: A single LLM call with no tools, validated and working, beats a half-built ReAct-plus-memory-plus-planning agent where you can't tell which piece is actually broken.

cards.heading: One agent, one clear responsibility
cards.hook: A SearchAgent that only searches is easier to build, test, and trust than a SuperAgent with an if/elif chain routing between search, analyze, and write.

cards.heading: Define tool and memory interfaces before you implement either
cards.hook: A Tool protocol with just name, description, and execute, agreed on before any concrete tool is written, is what lets you swap implementations later without touching the caller.

cards.heading: A structured prompt has named sections, not one wall of text
cards.hook: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS, AVAILABLE TOOLS, CONVERSATION HISTORY, CURRENT TASK, OUTPUT FORMAT as explicit labeled sections makes a long prompt something the model can navigate, not just scan.

cards.heading: Graceful degradation beats a single try/except around everything
cards.hook: Falling back to an alternative tool on error, a partial result on timeout, and only then a hard failure message is a ladder of fallbacks, not one all-or-nothing catch block.

cards.heading: Retry with exponential backoff, not a fixed delay
cards.hook: Doubling the wait between retries, and only on errors explicitly marked retryable, avoids hammering a struggling service while still giving a transient failure a chance to recover.

cards.heading: Validate at both boundaries, not just the input
cards.hook: Checking the task string on the way in catches malformed requests; checking the result structure on the way out catches an agent that silently produced garbage — most agents only do the first.

cards.heading: Cache by task, not just by raw LLM call
cards.hook: Hashing the task string as a cache key and short-circuiting identical requests avoids re-running an entire multi-step agent loop for a question it already answered minutes ago.

cards.heading: Independent subtasks are a parallelization opportunity most agents waste
cards.hook: If two steps in a plan don't depend on each other's output, running them concurrently cuts wall-clock time without changing the agent's actual reasoning at all.

cards.heading: Summarize context before it blows the token budget, not after
cards.hook: Checking token count against a threshold and summarizing proactively avoids a request silently failing because the prompt exceeded the model's context window.

cards.heading: Structured logs beat print statements for debugging an agent
cards.hook: Logging task started and task completed events with task, agent id, and timing as structured fields means you can actually query your logs later, not just scroll through them.

cards.heading: Route simple tasks to a cheaper model automatically
cards.hook: A short question can go to a cheap model; a request with analyze or compare in it routes to the expensive one — classifying complexity first keeps average cost down without hurting hard tasks.

cards.heading: A stable system prompt gets cached by the provider for free
cards.hook: Keeping the system prompt identical across calls and only varying the user task lets provider-side prompt caching kick in automatically — rewriting it per call throws that savings away.
